display_title: Official Review of Paper2755 by Reviewer HdYi

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper tunes the discounted factor for all agents by using a learning representation of uncertainty to update the utility networks of individual agents. Results on two environments shows that the performance of the proposed method is better than SOTA methods.
content.main_review:
The paper proposes an interesting idea that different agents should use different discounted factors. Although this idea is already proposed in the single agent setting, varying discounted factors in multi-agent setting is still interesting and novel in my opinion. I have some concerns listed as follows.

1. In the introduction part, authors use a soccer match example to show that agents would change their policies when their abilities change, which is attractive and reasonable. However, in the method and experiment parts, the problem is not mentioned or addressed. More specifically, the randomness of agents is fixed in the experiments and the method does not mention when to retrain the network that outputs discounted factors.
2. I do not understand why you assume that the policies are deterministic. For the stochastic policy, the problem that some agents would change their policies when their abilities change also exists. Is it possible to use the same methods for stochastic policies?
3. For the experiments, some details are ignored. How many runs are used to generate figures is unknown. The variance of the performance is not given. The seeds used in the experiment is unknown. The discounted factors of baselines are not provided.
The lack of details and codes make the paper hard to be reproduced.
4. Stochastic level of agents is fixed. It is not convincing by conducting experiments in one setting. I suggest that more settings should be considered or randomly generated.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In summary, 

1. The setting of the method and the experiment is not the same as the authors claim in the introduction.
2. The details of experiment are not provided. The results are not convincing.
3. The Stochastic level of agents is fixed and designed by authors, which is not convincing.

Overall, the idea is interesting and novel. However, the experiment and method still need to be improved.

content.title: Response to Reviewer HdYi
content.comment:
We first would like to thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and comments.

**In the introduction part, authors use a soccer match example to show that agents would change their policies when their abilities change, which is attractive and reasonable. However, in the method and experiment parts, the problem is not mentioned or addressed. More specifically, the randomness of agents is fixed in the experiments and the method does not mention when to retrain the network that outputs discounted factors.**

The soccer game was used to explain the context and relate to how human intelligence achieves collective goals by refactoring joint policies in such degraded circumstances. This was provided as motivation as to why machines need to emulate the same. As an example, please refer to the Robotic manufacturing use case in Industry 4.0. Now StarCraft is a similar game as soccer when it comes to needing collective coordination against an adversarial setting. May we point out here that 10 different experiments were conducted on StarCraft, each with a different combination of stochasticity/degradation. The learning representation was trained in one experiment and then reused for 9 other experiments where the degradation values changed completely. Please refer to figure 2.  Retraining of the learning representation (core proposition of DSDF) is not needed unless the number of agents changes. Retraining is needed only for agents’ utility networks which use the $θ_γ$ from the learning representation (which works across all values).

**I do not understand why you assume that the policies are deterministic. For the stochastic policy, the problem that some agents would change their policies when their abilities change also exists. Is it possible to use the same methods for stochastic policies?**


Thank you for the comment. Please note that the policy can be stochastic, in fact, it is stochastic. We used the word “deterministic” for agents in the sense, that the deterministic agents execute an action given by a stochastic policy with 100% probability. For “stochastic” agents, since they are degraded, they may not be executing an action that is given by the stochastic policy, they may execute a different action. Like if the policy tells it to move an arm 7 Degree towards the right, it might move 3/4/5 degrees to the right and sometimes 7 degrees to the right.  However, we realize the choice of the word “Stochastic” and “deterministic” for agents is confusing. Hence, we have changed the reference and now use “Noisy/Degraded” instead of stochastic and “Good/Accordant” instead of deterministic.

**For the experiments, some details are ignored. How many runs are used to generate figures is unknown. The variance of the performance is not given. The seeds used in the experiment is unknown. The discounted factors of baselines are not provided. The lack of details and codes make the paper hard to be reproduced.**

All the relevant details on Std dev and seeds are now provided. Also, we included all the necessary details in the appendix section. 

**Stochastic level of agents is fixed. It is not convincing by conducting experiments in one setting. I suggest that more settings should be considered or randomly generated.**

As highlighted above, the experiments were conducted for 10 different settings of stochasticity/noise. Now we have validated the same for three different scenarios in the StarCraft environment, and for every 10 different experiments performed at different stochasticity levels of the agents.

replying_to: Replying to DSDF: Coordinated look-ahead strategy in stochastic multi-agent reinforcement learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper2755 by Reviewer Kino

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a method to handle stochastic (noisy) agents by tuning the discount factor during training. Agents that are stochastic learn to use a lower value of the discount factor which in turn changes their RL objective to one of a shorter horizon.
content.main_review:
At its current version, the paper has major issues which are detailed below.

- The overview of the existing literature is lacking.
	- Issues with the literature description begin in the first paragraph: e.g. (Foerster et al, 2018a) is not learning a centralised policy (and it is the same citation to Foerster et al, 2018b)
	- Paragraph #3 discussing CDTE is unfinished
	- Literature discussion focuses only on CTDE methods. CTDE is an established paradigm and there should not be a need to motivate it. I would expect to see at least a discussion on stochasticity, and on changing the discount factor during training.
	- I believe the paper would benefit from a "Related Work" which can help place it in the existing literature.


- The use of the term "stochastic/deterministic" agent is confusing.
	- Stochastic policies have a different meaning in RL. There are even cases where a stochastic policy can be an optimal policy (e.g. rock-paper-scissors). I believe the authors mean to introduce noise to the actions of some agents, but the term deterministic/stochastic is not correct. Even in the case of the paper's experiments, the policies followed by the "deterministic" agents are actually stochastic since they use epsilon-greedy.

- The method tunes the discount factor
	- In the background section (and in the literature) the discount factor is treated as part of the Dec-POMDP definition. Changing this factor directly changes the nature of the problem and influences the learning objective. I would be open in discussing if this is a valid approach in the first place, but I would at least expect a discussion of the literature on the subject.

- The experiments 
	- SMAC/2s3z is a relatively simple environment. The original unmodified version is solved by most algorithms including QMIX/IQL (as shown in Papoudakis et al, 2021). By adding noise to the actions of the agent the environment becomes harder: but how does, in practice, the optimal policy change? I would expect the agents still need to focus their attacks on specific enemies, (and the noisy agents should do their best to also focus their attacks). However, in QMIX/IQL the agents do not seem to learn to solve this environment. Does DSDF learn a different behaviour than the one I described?
	- I disagree that LBF "does not require much collaboration..." (caption Fig4). LBF requires agents to move together towards a food item and simultaneously try to load it. There is no reward if the agents do not manage to do this. In contrast, SMAC (especially easier tasks such as 2s3z) is much more lenient in agents not collaborating for a certain amount of time (an agent moving further away, an agent trying to independently kill an opponent, etc).
	- I would expect multiple seeds and plots that include std across seeds. The argument "In this case study, we skipped doing multiple experiments as we thought they are redundant" (page 6/first sentence) is not convincing. Especially in RL/MARL where different seeds can lead to significantly different results.
content.summary_of_the_review: There are a few major issues with the motivation of the method which leads me to recommend the rejection of this paper.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2755 by Reviewer Kino

content.title: Response to Reviewer Kino
content.comment:
We first would like to thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and comments.

**The overview of the existing literature is lacking.**

* We thank the reviewer for detailed comments on the literature description. The citation for Foerster et al, 2019a, is now fixed. The unfinished CTDE paragraph is also deleted. Apologize for the inadvertent error.

* CTDE discussion is now compressed, and robotic manufacturing example is expanded for motivation. Please note there is very limited related work on this topic of changing discounted factor due to stochasticity/noise in the multi-agent scenario and hence the limited mention. There exists some literature for the single-agent scenario, but the problem of coordination is non-existent in that and hence we presume it is not related to our work.

**The use of the term "stochastic/deterministic" agent is confusing.**

Thank you for the suggestion. Stochastic agents (defined as one which takes a random action with a certain probability as opposed to one given by policy) are now refereed as Degraded/ Noisy agents while deterministic agents are referred to as Good/Accordant agents.

**The method tunes the discount factor**

In the background section, we have given the traditional MARL problem, and hence discounted factor is treated as part of the Dec-POMDP definition. We agree changing the discounted factor changes the nature of the problem. In the literature, we could not find any similar works which deal with changing discounted factor and/or handling noisy agents in multi-agent reinforcement learning. To the best of our knowledge, we are the ones who are proposing the method to handle a combination of noisy and accordant agents. 

**The experiments**

* Yes, we agree that the original SMAC/2s3z environment is solved by QMIX/IQL trained agents. However, when the agents are noisy, the agents will take different actions than those instructed by the policy.  In this case, the update of the value function network will be poor as the agent is unaware of the wrong action taken and this error is propagated to further time steps. However, in our proposed approach the discounted factor is altered such that the agent look-ahead strategy is changed. For noisy agents, they will focus on immediate rewards i.e., they will kill enemies only if they are nearby/sure shot of killing whereas the accordant agents travel lot/create a strategy to kill enemies. This sort of different behavior the agents will learn using the proposed DSDF approach. In the QMIX/IQL, the agents will focus on traveling long distances and killing enemies regardless of the noisy characteristics they have. Hence, they will underperform which is evident from the results we have given in the paper. Also, it should be noted that we also performed experiments on two more SMAC environments (8m, 1c_3s_5z) and we observed the proposed DSDF approach achieves good collaboration when compared with existing methods. 


* We understand the perspective given by the reviewer. What was meant here, in LBF if there are some sub-optimal actions, there is still window to recoup losses. However, SMAC is much more unforgiving where a sub-optimal action can result in the agent getting killed. The collaboration required in LBF and SMAC are slightly different and the manifestation of sub-optimal policy can create longer episodes in LBF while it could be a loss in SMAC. We agree that LBF does require some very sound collaboration and notably the DSDF method is able to achieve it in presence of noisy agents also.

* Std across plots is now included.  Also please note that three SMAC settings are now used and in each setting 10 different experiments are performed using varying degrees of degradation across agents. Note that the Learning representation of discounted factor needs to be learned only once and then reused in rest 9 different experiments. We agree the  need for different seeds in MARL environments. Hence we have now included the std plots for both SMAC and LBF environments.

content.comment:
Thank you for addressing my comments. I believe the additional experiments already improved the paper. Also, the use of "noisy" and "accordant" agents, while not necessarily the best choice, should make the intentions of the authors more clear. That said, I am still concerned about the placement of this paper within the existing literature. 

In addition, the answer to reviewer "j88F" on "calculating the optimal \gamma" and " modelling the stochasticity of the other agents directly" is not satisfactory. The authors use a heuristic to calculate \gamma values, and therefore I would hope to see that the proposed approach can outperform other solutions to this problem (like modelling the stochasticity). Due to this narrow approach to the problem noted by the other reviewers I have decided not to increase my score.

content.title: Response to Reviwer Kino
content.comment:
Thank you for your time. We respect your decision and appreciate you taking the time to re-review.

It is important to point out that we are NOT using heuristics to calculate $\gamma$ values. In fact, the core proposition of the paper is a method to formulate a Learning Representation to calculate $\gamma$ values for each agent. The only place where heuristics is used refers to the situation where the behavior of agents changes continuously and there we use heuristics to decide WHEN to retrain the model (specifically the Agent’s network and NOT the learning representation for $\gamma$ which still remains valid).

The fact that our method outperforms other available methods, in given settings, is demonstrated through experiments given in the paper. As the reviewer rightly pointed out it would be interesting to compare the proposed approach with other solutions like stochasticity modeling. However, we feel the stochastic model-based approach cannot be generalized to the different domains as it requires domain expertise which leads to significant human effort to arrive at the stochasticity model. On the other hand, we feel the proposed approach can be extended to multiple domains in a straightforward manner.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of centralized multi-agent training. The paper claims that a problem that arises in multi-agent training is when agents slowly become more stochastic over time (aging robots). To address this issue, the paper proposes to learn separate discount factors for each agent in a way that considers the discount factors for other agents.
content.main_review:
The problem motivation is rather unconvincing. Sure, there can be drift along many axes over time in multi-agent training (non-stationarity, swapping of roles...), so I'm confused as to why the paper focuses on this very narrow problem of increased stochasticity. A lot of multi-agent domains are AI agents that don't decay over time. Even in robotics settings, is there any support for whether deteriorating components will affect *collaboration* (I can see it affecting control mostly, but not so much collaboration)?

On a related note, it seems excessively narrow that the paper is only focusing on learning separate discount factors for each agent. There seems to be many possible ways to address the proposed problem, the most natural of which seems to be modeling the stochasticity of the other agents directly!

Another question I have is, Section 3.1 title is "...Calculate Optimal \gamma", but the proposed solutions all seem to be heuristics ("with every mismatch we will decrease the discount factor"). Why does the paper claim to be calculating the optimal \gamma? Is it even feasible (computationally) to compute the optimal \gamma?

Lastly, the writing is really, really poor, and is littered with grammar mistakes, and incomplete sentences. I find the writing unacceptable for a scientific publication.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem motivation is unsatisfactory, since the problem seems too narrow (only focusing on decay in stochasticity) and unrealistic, and the proposed solution is also unnecessarily narrow (only looks at tweaking discount factors). None of these choices are justified particularly well, so the overall contribution is really difficult to pinpoint. Lastly, the writing needs to be greatly improved.

content.title: Response to Reviewer j88F
content.comment:
We first would like to thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and comments.

**The problem motivation is rather unconvincing. Sure, there can be drift along many axes over time in multi-agent training (non-stationarity, swapping of roles...), so I'm confused as to why the paper focuses on this very narrow problem of increased stochasticity. A lot of multi-agent domains are AI agents that don't decay over time. Even in robotics settings, is there any support for whether deteriorating components will affect collaboration (I can see it affecting control mostly, but not so much collaboration)? On a related note, it seems excessively narrow that the paper is only focusing on learning separate discount factors for each agent. There seems to be many possible ways to address the proposed problem, the most natural of which seems to be modeling the stochasticity of the other agents directly!**

The motivation of the problem stems from Industry 4.0 use cases, especially the ones enabled by 5G. The low latency communication of 5G enables precise coordination among machines on the shop floor. Often some machines may get degraded whereby they cannot execute the action always given by policy. This results in the partial breakdown of collaboration as in a multi-agent scenario each agent needs to “stick to a plan” in order to achieve an effective global return. This results in the need for frequent maintenance and thus loss of productivity. Please refer to this link, which gives an idea about the extent of maintenance operations( daily/500 hrs/5000+ hrs) which need to be done for each robot [1]. Now in the coming days, as multiple robots start collaborating, the maintenance need will increase manyfold. 

Please also refer to Section 5 in [2] which talks about the applications of Multi-Robot assembly and challenges of synchronization in multi-robot coordination.  The study also points specifically “Such coordination requires extensive communication, both implicit and explicit, to accommodate changes in the environment, task, and behaviors of other robotic agents [2]”.

Notably, our paper proposes a framework that will enable us to address such changes – which in our case is “behavior of other robotic agents”. In that sense, we believe our paper, though a bit futuristic, could be very applicable to low latency collaborative manufacturing use cases of the future.

Our principal contribution is about creating a learning representation, which could provide relative discounted factors to each agent based on its performance so that the global collaboration could be impacted by the least possible amount. Please note the learning representation, once trained can be used for varying degrees of degradation.

The deteriorating performance will affect collaboration since in partial observability settings, where agents cannot see another’s action or rewards, the collaboration depends on sticking to a plan which is devised mutually during training. The same is also proven through the sub-par performance of QMIX on degraded settings as compared to DSDF. Also please note modeling the stochasticity of other agents’ performance is challenging in the partial observable environments since the action & reward of another agent is not visible. And in circumstances when it is visible, modeling the same might not be scalable due to communication bottleneck.

**Another question I have is, Section 3.1 title is "...Calculate Optimal \gamma", but the proposed solutions all seem to be heuristics ("with every mismatch we will decrease the discount factor"). Why does the paper claim to be calculating the optimal \gamma? Is it even feasible (computationally) to compute the optimal \gamma?**

We agree on the concern on the use of the word “optimal”. We have changed it to “more effective”, i.e something which is better than available ones.

**Lastly, the writing is really, really poor, and is littered with grammar mistakes, and incomplete sentences. I find the writing unacceptable for a scientific publication.**

Regarding English skills, we humbly acknowledge our deficiency in English. We have reworked the sentence/grammar throughout the paper. We request you to relook at the same in light of the changed (hopefully improved 😊 )  writing.

[1] https://www.sdcautomation.com/blog/preventative-maintenance-for-industrial-robots/

[2] Marvel, Jeremy & Bostelman, Roger & Falco, Joseph. (2018). Multi-Robot Assembly Strategies and Metrics. ACM Computing Surveys. 51. 1-32.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2755 by Reviewer 7seM

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses the problem of how to deal with stochasticity of the agents when they work with other agents. Stochasticity is assumed to happen over time, as result of degradation of the agents (e.g., robots that fail). The approach proposed learns a representation of the uncertainty and assigns to the stochastic agents tasks that are simpler and closer by while assigning to the deterministic agents more complex tasks.  A step function is used for the stochastic agents to change their behavior, which simplifies the retraining.  The proposed method (DSDF) computes a discount factor for all the agents simultaneously. The paper proposes also another method, iterative penalization method, which does not perform as well as DSDF, but is simple. The methods proposed are compared to other approaches in two different benchmark environments, StarCraft and a Foraging environments,  and show improved results.
content.main_review:
The method proposed is described well, with an outline of the DSDF algorithm used and with details in Appendix on the parameters used.  The method is relatively simple and appears to perform well. In the StarCraft experiments, the degree of stochasticity varies from 0 to 0.6. Since the number of agents is limited to 6, and only 3 agents out of 6  are stochastic, the experiments are not fully convincing. Larger problems would be appropriate to increase the quality of the experimental results presented.  
It is not clear how important the problem is in real applications and if the solution proposed will work as well in real applications.  How important is to address the proposed problem is also not clear. In the robotics example shown the proposed approach is useful, but still it remain to be seen if the approach scales up to real environments and problems,. The choice of a step function to compute the discount factor makes the approach less realistic. It would make sense to look at how robots tend to degrade and apply them, to see if they provide any new insight .
First line of Section 3: "more optimal joint policy" is not quite right, since nothing can be better than the optimal policy!

content.title: Response to Reviewer 7seM
content.comment:
We first would like to thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and comments.

**The method proposed is described well, with an outline of the DSDF algorithm used and with details in the Appendix on the parameters used. The method is relatively simple and appears to perform well. In the StarCraft experiments, the degree of stochasticity varies from 0 to 0.6. Since the number of agents is limited to 6, and only 3 agents out of 6 are stochastic, the experiments are not fully convincing. Larger problems would be appropriate to increase the quality of the experimental results presented.**

Please note that for the StarCraft environment the map 2s_3z was used using 10 different experiment settings where each setting had a different combination of agent stochasticity. Also, some of the agents have a stochasticity value up to 0.86 (please refer to Fig. 2a in the original paper). In addition to the same, now two more map scenarios (which have more number of agents) were added – 8m and 1c_3s_5z. So, till now, the proposed approach is tested for the case up to 9 agents out of which upto 6 agents are noisy (1c_3s_5z).  All the results, including the ones on new environments, are updated in the paper. 

**It is not clear how important the problem is in real applications and if the solution proposed will work as well in real applications. How important is to address the proposed problem is also not clear. In the robotics example shown the proposed approach is useful, but still it remain to be seen if the approach scales up to real environments and problems,. The choice of a step function to compute the discount factor makes the approach less realistic. It would make sense to look at how robots tend to degrade and apply them, to see if they provide any new insight .**

With respect to the applicability of the problem in real-life application, may we point out, that the same is quite pertinent to the Industry 4.0 scenario, where a certain agent in a factory floor could get degraded and as a result, the entire output of the floor would be affected till the degraded agent is changed.

 Leveraging our proposed method, the degraded agents could be used to their limited capability while the other agents can take up longer trajectory jobs and thereby compensate, in parts, for the degraded ones. Such a mechanism could reduce the frequency of maintenance and thereby the total downtime in a factory floor.  In [1], the discussion refers to the frequency of maintenance in industrial robots, which needs to be done daily, every 600 hours, and every 5000 hours. We believe, our method has the potential to reduce a good part of these maintenance hours thereby saving cost. The need and complexity of managing multiple synchronized robots on a factory floor is also discussed in Section 5 of [2]. 

Regarding step function assumption in degradation, it may be noted that this is not a limitation in using the discounted factor learning representation. If the degradation changes significantly, then only the agent’s utility networks (as part of QMIX) will need incremental retraining, but the discount factor learning representation would remain valid. To illustrate this point, we had conducted 10 different experiments (in SMAC environment) using different agent degradation values /combinations as shown in figure 2. However, the learning representation of discounted factor was trained only in experiment No. 1 and then reused in the other 9 experiments. The collaborative performance in all the 9 experiments obtained using the trained learning representation (DSDF) as seen from Figure 3 is outperforms the existing methods. However, an open problem is to identify the threshold, when the degradation changes significantly to necessitate agent utility network re-training which motivates us to consider degradation as a step function rather than a continuous function.  We recommend this problem for future exploration. 

**First line of Section 3: "more optimal joint policy" is not quite right, since nothing can be better than the optimal policy!**

We agree on the comment on “more optimal policy” and have now changed the same to “more effective policy”.

The clarification on the language, .i.e. "noisy agent" instead of "stochastic", and "accordant agent" instead of "deterministic agent", does not make the paper much more clear. replying_to: Replying to Thanks for the answers and clarifications

content.title: Response to Reviwer 7seM
content.comment:
Thank You for your valuable comments. Appreciate you taking time out to re-review our changes. You have rightly pointed out the importance of situations where agents could be in hundreds. Please note in such a situation the entire CTDE based approach may not be valid. The centralized training requires agents to communicate their local observations to the centralized system. In an environment that has hundreds of agents, such a communication method imposes a severe bottleneck. Hence in such circumstances methods like Coordinated Reinforcement Learning [1] that use “interaction locality” to reduce communication or methods inspired from Mean-Field Theory [2] may be necessary. However such methods depend on an approximation of “interaction locality” and hence do not perform in all scenarios especially when the number of agents is not that large but the task requires finer coordination.

Also please note that this is the first time such a problem of agent degradation is being attempted. The problem of getting the right $\gamma$ values for a modified lookahead strategy was addressed here through a learning representation-based method.  Hence while scalability by a factor of hundreds could indeed be a bottleneck here, the same will be explored with alternate methods in our subsequent work.

[1] Zhang, Chongjie and Victor R. Lesser. “Coordinating multi-agent reinforcement learning with limited communication.” AAMAS (2013).

[2] Yang, Yaodong, Rui Luo, Minne Li, Ming Zhou, Weinan Zhang, and Jun Wang. "Mean field multi-agent reinforcement learning." In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 5571-5580. PMLR, 2018.

content.title: General response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback on the paper. We have worked on the feedback received and have made the following  changes to the paper. 

1. **Additional Experiments**: We have performed the evaluation of the proposed approach on two additional map scenarios in the SMAC environment and listed the results in the paper.  Significant improvement was observed when compared to existing methods for both these complex scenarios. 

2. **Renamed the stochastic agents**: We see some confusion regarding the usage of the term "stochastic agent" vs "stochastic policy". We reiterate that the policy is stochastic for us. Accordingly, the term "stochastic agent" is changed to "noisy agent" as they perform noisy (random) actions with some probability against the one instructed by the policy. Also, the term "deterministic agent" has been changed to "accordant agent".
